newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Car price gaps show need for single currency - EU.
newsitem.headline: Car price gaps show need for single currency - EU.

text.p: The soaring pound has led to record price differences for cars in the EU, the European Commission said on Friday, stressing that this underlined the need for a single currency.
The gap between the lowest and the highest price in the EU had widened since late last year for several popular car models, the European Union executive said.
To take just one example, someone buying a Peugeot 306 would need to pay 37.6 percent more in Britain than in the Netherlands, according to the Commission's survey.
"It has to be noted that the widening price gap has been due to currency movements, rather than to changes in recommended retail prices in the member states concerned," it said.

Because of the stronger pound, on May 1 Britain had the highest prices in the EU for 54 of the 75 best-selling models, measured in European currency units, compared to only 15 in the previous report in November. Several car makers had not cut their prices on the British market, despite the firmer pound.
The pound has rallied 30 percent against the German mark over the last year, surging to a six-year high on Friday.
In contrast, in Germany and France prices were the highest for only 11 car models. Twenty-four models were cheapest in the Netherlands, followed by Portugal with 18 models.
A single European currency was the only way to avoid exchange rate movements causing price differences incompatible with the bloc's single market, the Commission said.
"It should also ensure that prices are determined solely by economic factors," it said in a statement.
Under the 1992 Maastricht treaty, economic and monetary union (EMU) is due to be launched on January 1, 1999, with those EU countries which meet tough economic criteria.
However, the Commission's statement did not mention that Britain can opt out from EMU and that London looks unlikely to join from the start.

On May 1, price differences on cars across the EU exceeded 20 percent for 53 of the 75 models examined. This applied especially to models of Italy's Fiat, France's Citroen and Renault, of U.S. giant Ford, Germany's VW, and of Japan's Mitsubishi and Subaru.

"Manufacturers such as the BMW group, Mercedes-Benz, and Audi as well as most of the Japanese producers, apparently apply a pricing policy across the Community aimed at keeping their prices within a certain margin," the Commission said.

Comparing May 1 with November 1, the difference between the highest and lowest price in the EU increased to 33.9 percent from 26.8 percent for a Ford Fiesta, to 30.9 from 21.1 for a VW Golf and to 24.7 from 15.7 for a BMW 316, the survey showed.
"In the period under investigation, currency fluctuations were relatively extensive," the Commission said.
The British and the Irish pounds continued to rise, by 9.3 and 2.5 percent respectively against the ecu, while all other currencies weakened.
Despite the appreciating pound, only Ford, Renault, Peugeot and Seat cut their prices in Britain.
"The majority of the other manufacturers have increased or maintained their prices, thus benefiting from the so-called 'windfall profits' resulting from the revaluation of the pound."
